concrete_modulus_of_elasticity.title: Modulus of Elasticity of Concrete — Static & Time-Dependent
concrete_modulus_of_elasticity.description: The secant modulus of elasticity of concrete at 28 days and its variation with age. Used in deflection calculations, stress distribution, dynamic analysis, and compatibility checks between concrete and steel. Codes differ significantly in how they define and calculate this value.
concrete_modulus_of_elasticity.keywords: modulus of elasticity elastic modulus Ecm Ec Young's modulus stiffness concrete stiffness time dependent modulus Ec variation with time concrete elastic modulus formula

standards.notes: EC2 gives the most complete treatment — a 28-day value plus explicit time evolution. The s-coefficient for cement type is critical: rapid hardening cement gains 90% of Ecm within 7 days while slow hardening cement may take 28+ days. This matters for propping, formwork striking, and prestress transfer calculations. The formula is calibrated to normal weight concrete (density ~2400 kg/m³) — for lightweight concrete use the density-modified formula in Clause 11.3.2.
standards.limits: Ecm ranges from 27 GPa (C16/20) to 44 GPa (C90/105). For dynamic analysis, use tangent modulus Ec = 1.05 × Ecm.
standards.notation: **Ecm** = Secant modulus of elasticity at 28 days (GPa) | **fcm** = Mean compressive strength = fck + 8 MPa | **Ecm(t)** = Modulus at age t days | **fcm(t)** = Mean strength at age t days | **s** = Cement type coefficient: 0.20 for CEM 42.5R/52.5 (rapid hardening); 0.25 for CEM 42.5N (normal); 0.38 for CEM 32.5N (slow hardening) | **t** = Age of concrete in days | **Example M35**: fcm = 35+8 = 43 MPa → Ecm = 22×(43/10)^0.3 = 33.7 GPa

standards.notes: The IS 456 formula is simple and widely used but gives values approximately 10–15% lower than EC2 for equivalent grades. For M35 (cube): IS gives 29.6 GPa; EC2 for C28/35 (equivalent cylinder grade) gives 32.3 GPa. The difference matters in deflection calculations — IS 456 slightly underestimates stiffness, leading to slightly conservative deflections. The complete absence of a time-dependent formula is a significant gap: engineers must use IS 456 Annex C (simplified method) or reference IS 1343 for age-at-loading effects.
standards.limits: Short-term static modulus only. For sustained loading, effective modulus Ec,eff = Ec/(1+θ) where θ is creep coefficient.
standards.notation: **Ec** = Short-term static modulus of elasticity (MPa) | **fck** = Characteristic cube compressive strength (MPa) | **Example M35**: Ec = 5000√35 = 29,580 MPa ≈ 29.6 GPa | **Note**: IS 456 gives NO time-dependent formula — age effects handled indirectly through creep coefficient in serviceability checks

standards.notes: IRC 112 adopts the EC2 formula unchanged — making it directly compatible with EC2-designed international bridges. However the time-dependent component is particularly important for bridge design: integral bridges, cantilever construction, cable-stayed bridges, and long-span prestressed beams all require accurate Ecm(t) at transfer. For bridge design in India, always use IRC 112's formula — never IS 456's simplified formula.
standards.limits: Same range as EC2. Time-dependent formula mandatory for bridges where age at loading is critical (e.g. staged construction, prestress transfer).
standards.notation: **Ecm** = Secant modulus at 28 days (GPa) | **fcm** = Mean cylinder strength = fck + 8 MPa | **Ecm(t)** = Modulus at age t (same formula as EC2) | **s** = Cement coefficient same as EC2 | **Note**: IRC 112 uses cylinder fck unlike IS 456 which uses cube fck — critical distinction when converting between the two

standards.notes: ACI gives the lowest Ec values of all codes for equivalent concrete grades — because it is calibrated to cylinder strength which is lower than cube strength. For f'c=28 MPa (cylinder), ACI gives Ec=24.9 GPa; IS M35 gives 29.6 GPa; EC2 C25/30 (equivalent to ~28 MPa cylinder) gives 31.5 GPa. ACI 363R provides a modified formula for high-strength concrete (f'c > 40 MPa): Ec = (3320√f'c + 6900) MPa — significantly higher than the standard formula at high strengths.
standards.limits: Valid for concrete density between 1440 and 2560 kg/m³. For f'c > 40 MPa, use measured Ec or refined formula from ACI 363R.
standards.formula: E_c = 0.043 \, w_c^{1.5} \sqrt{f'_c} \quad (\text{MPa}) \\ E_c = 4700 \sqrt{f'_c} \quad (\text{MPa, normal weight only})
standards.notation: **Ec** = Modulus of elasticity (MPa) | **wc** = Unit weight of concrete (kg/m³) — use 2320 for normal weight | **f'c** = Specified compressive strength — cylinder (MPa) | **Normal weight simplification**: wc = 2320 kg/m³ → 0.043×2320^1.5×√f'c ≈ 4730√f'c ≈ 4700√f'c | **Example f'c=28 MPa**: Ec = 4700√28 = 24,870 MPa ≈ 24.9 GPa

standards.notes: AASHTO's formula differs from ACI by using an exponent of 2.0 on density instead of 1.5, and 0.33 on strength instead of 0.5. This was introduced because research on bridge concretes (often higher density aggregates) showed ACI underestimated stiffness. The K1 regional factor allows calibration to local aggregate sources — important for long-span bridges where stiffness governs design more than strength.
standards.limits: For 0.1 ≤ f'c ≤ 0.105 GPa and 1440 ≤ wc ≤ 2500 kg/m³.
standards.notation: **K1** = Correction factor for regional aggregate stiffness = 1.0 unless determined from physical testing | **wc** = Unit weight of concrete (kg/m³) | **f'c** = Specified compressive strength (MPa) | **Note**: AASHTO uses wc^2.0 exponent vs ACI's wc^1.5 — gives more weight to concrete density | **Normal weight wc=2320**: Ec ≈ 4800√f'c MPa (slightly higher than ACI for same f'c)

standards.notes: DNV adopts the EC2 formula without modification. For offshore structures, the dynamic modulus (used in natural frequency and wave load calculations) is taken as Edyn = 1.05 × Ecm — a 5% increase. This is important for wind turbine gravity base foundations and offshore platform deck structures where resonance assessment requires accurate stiffness.
standards.limits: Normal weight concrete. For lightweight aggregate concrete, apply density correction.
standards.notation: **Ecm** = Secant modulus at 28 days | **fcm** = Mean cylinder strength | **Same formula as EC2** — DNV explicitly adopts EC2 Clause 3.1.3 | **Density correction**: Ecm,LWC = Ecm × (ρ/2400)^2 for lightweight concrete

concrete_compressive_strength.title: Concrete Compressive Strength — Characteristic, Mean & Design Values
concrete_compressive_strength.keywords: compressive strength fck fcd fcm f'c fcu characteristic strength design strength mean strength cylinder cube M25 M30 M35 C25/30 concrete grade
concrete_compressive_strength.description: Defines the characteristic compressive strength (fck), mean value (fcm), and design compressive strength (fcd). Critical distinction: cube vs cylinder specimens — this affects all derived material properties.

standards.limits: Minimum fck = 12 MPa (C12/15). Maximum fck = 90 MPa (C90/105). Standard range C20/25 to C50/60 for most structures.
standards.formula:
f_cm = f_ck + 8  (MPa)
f_cd = alpha_cc * f_ck / gamma_c = 0.85 * f_ck / 1.5
standards.notation: **fck** = Characteristic cylinder strength at 28 days (MPa) | **fcm** = Mean strength = fck + 8 MPa | **fcd** = Design compressive strength | **alpha_cc** = 0.85 (long-term factor; UK NA uses 1.0 for flexure) | **gamma_c** = 1.5 (partial safety factor for concrete) | **C25/30** = cylinder/cube notation
standards.notes: Global baseline. Cylinder strength used throughout. The +8 MPa rule for mean strength is empirical but well validated. Always check applicable National Annex for alpha_cc — UK uses 1.0 for flexure giving 11% higher design strength.

standards.limits: Minimum fck = 20 MPa for RCC (M20). Aggressive exposure: M30 minimum. Prestressed: M30 minimum. Max commonly specified: M60.
standards.notation: **fck** = Characteristic compressive strength of 150mm cube at 28 days (MPa) | **0.67** = Cube-to-in-situ conversion factor | **1.5** = Partial safety factor gamma_m | **fcd** = Design compressive strength for stress block calculations
standards.notes: IS 456 uses cube strength — opposite convention to Eurocode. The 0.67 factor converts cube to equivalent cylinder and accounts for sustained loading in one step. For M35: fcd = 0.67x35/1.5 = 15.6 MPa — nearly identical to EC2 for equivalent grade once cube-cylinder conversion is understood.

standards.limits: Minimum fck = 30 MPa for RCC bridge elements. Minimum fck = 35 MPa for prestressed concrete. Maximum fck = 65 MPa.
standards.formula:
f_cm = f_ck + Delta_f
f_cd = alpha_cc * f_ck / gamma_c = 0.67 * f_ck / 1.5
standards.notation: **fck** = Characteristic cylinder strength (NOTE: IRC 112 uses cylinder unlike IS 456) | **Delta_f** = 8 MPa for fck <= 50 MPa | **alpha_cc** = 0.67 in IRC 112 (more conservative than EC2's 0.85) | **gamma_c** = 1.5
standards.notes: IRC 112 uses alpha_cc = 0.67 instead of EC2's 0.85 — 21% more conservative. For C35 bridge concrete: IRC 112 gives fcd = 15.6 MPa vs EC2's 19.8 MPa. Always use alpha_cc = 0.67 for IRC 112, never 0.85.

standards.limits: Minimum f'c = 17 MPa for structural concrete. Seismic categories D-F: minimum 21 MPa. Special moment frames: 21 MPa min, 35 MPa max for lightweight.
standards.formula:
f'_c = specified cylinder strength at 28 days
f_bar'_c = f'_c + 1.34s  (required mean for mix design)
standards.notation: **f'c** = Specified compressive strength, 150x300mm cylinder (MPa) | **f-bar'c** = Required mean strength for mix proportioning | **s** = Standard deviation of test results | **Note** = ACI uses phi (capacity reduction) factors on final capacity — NOT a material fcd
standards.notes: ACI philosophy differs fundamentally: keeps nominal f'c in formulae and reduces final capacity by phi factors (0.65–0.90 by failure mode). Only compare final design capacity to EC2 — not intermediate stress values. ACI generally less conservative on concrete strength than EC2 for normal-strength concrete.

standards.limits: Minimum f'c = 16 MPa non-prestressed. Minimum f'c = 28 MPa prestressed. Maximum f'c = 105 MPa for high-strength provisions.
standards.formula:
f'_c = 28-day cylinder strength (MPa)
f'_ci = concrete strength at time of initial prestress
standards.notation: **f'c** = Specified compressive strength (MPa) — cylinder | **f'ci** = Concrete strength at prestress transfer | **lambda** = Concrete density modification factor (1.0 normal weight) | **Note** = AASHTO uses phi-factor approach like ACI — no separate fcd
standards.notes: AASHTO follows ACI philosophy — cylinder strength, phi-factor approach. Bridge-specific minimum of 28 MPa for prestressed is more stringent than ACI. For f'c > 70 MPa, AASHTO imposes limits on shear and flexure formulae — recognising standard empirical equations become unreliable at very high strengths.

standards.limits: Minimum fck = 25 MPa. Offshore structures typically 40–70 MPa. Maximum fck = 85 MPa within standard provisions.
standards.formula:
f_cd = f_ck / gamma_c
gamma_c = 1.5 (normal) or 1.65 (offshore ULS)
standards.notation: **fck** = Characteristic cylinder compressive strength (MPa) | **fcd** = Design compressive strength | **gamma_c** = 1.5 normal; 1.65 offshore ULS (consequence of failure) | **alpha_cc** = Not separately defined — long-term effects included in gamma_c calibration
standards.notes: DNV uses highest gamma_c = 1.65 for offshore ULS — reflects harsh exposure, difficulty of inspection and repair offshore, and catastrophic consequences of failure. For C40 offshore: fcd = 40/1.65 = 24.2 MPa vs EC2's 22.7 MPa — similar despite different routes.

standards.limits: Grade C25 to C50 for most applications. C60 and above treated as high strength with additional checks.
standards.notation: **fcu** = Characteristic compressive strength of 100mm or 150mm cube at 28 days (MPa) | **0.67** = In-situ to cube ratio | **gamma_m** = 1.5 | **Note** = BS 8110 superseded by EC2 in UK but still used in Hong Kong, Malaysia, Singapore
standards.notes: BS 8110 formula identical to IS 456 — IS 456 was historically derived from BS 8110. Key difference: BS 8110 uses 100mm cubes which give ~5% higher strength than IS 456's 150mm cubes. Formally superseded in UK from 2010 but still specified on legacy projects.

concrete_creep_shrinkage.title: Creep & Shrinkage of Concrete
concrete_creep_shrinkage.keywords: creep shrinkage creep coefficient phi shrinkage strain long term deflection autogenous drying effective modulus age at loading relative humidity notional size h0
concrete_creep_shrinkage.description: Creep is the increase in strain under sustained stress over time. Shrinkage is volumetric reduction independent of loading. Both cause long-term deflection, loss of prestress, redistribution of forces, and restraint stresses.

standards.limits: Creep coefficient phi(inf,t0) typically 1.0–3.5 normal conditions. RH < 40% or h0 < 100mm: creep can exceed 5.0.
standards.formula:
phi(t,t0) = phi_0 * beta_c(t,t0)
phi_0 = phi_RH * beta(fcm) * beta(t0)
beta(fcm) = 16.8 / sqrt(fcm)
beta(t0) = 1 / (0.1 + t0^0.20)
eps_cs = eps_cd + eps_ca
eps_ca(inf) = 2.5*(fck - 10) * 10^-6
standards.notation: **phi(t,t0)** = Creep coefficient at time t loaded at t0 | **phi0** = Notional creep coefficient | **phi_RH** = Factor for relative humidity | **beta(fcm)** = Factor for concrete strength | **beta(t0)** = Factor for age at loading | **eps_cs** = Total shrinkage | **eps_cd** = Drying shrinkage | **eps_ca** = Autogenous shrinkage | **h0** = Notional size = 2Ac/u (mm) | **s** = Cement type: 0.20 rapid hardening / 0.25 normal / 0.38 slow
standards.notes: Most rigorous model. Autogenous shrinkage significant for fck > 35 MPa. Ignoring autogenous (as IS 456 does) can underestimate total shrinkage by 30–40% for M50+ concrete. Annex B needs 6 inputs: RH, h0, fcm, t0, t, cement type.

standards.limits: Creep coefficient valid for loading after 7 days minimum. Shrinkage strain applicable after 28 days.
standards.formula:
theta = 2.2 (loading at 7 days)
theta = 1.6 (loading at 28 days)
theta = 1.1 (loading at 1 year)
E_c,eff = E_c / (1 + theta)
eps_cs = 0.0003 (total, unrestrained)
standards.notation: **theta** = Ultimate creep coefficient from Table 2 — function of age at loading only | **Ec,eff** = Effective modulus accounting for creep | **eps_cs** = Ultimate shrinkage strain = 300e-6 (single value — no humidity or size dependence)
standards.notes: Extremely simplified. Single shrinkage strain 300e-6 reasonable for Indian conditions (RH 60–70%) but unconservative for thin sections in coastal areas or HSC. Creep coefficients (2.2, 1.6, 1.1) broadly align with EC2 for RH=50%, h0=150mm. For important structures use IS 1343 or EC2 model directly.

standards.limits: Valid for 40% <= RH <= 100%, 100mm <= h0 <= 500mm, t0 >= 1 day. For RH < 40% use Annex A-2 detailed method.
standards.formula:
phi(inf,t0) = phi_RH * beta(fcm) * beta(t0)
eps_cs = eps_cd0 * k_h + eps_ca(inf)
[Same formulae as EC2 Annex B]
standards.notation: **phi(inf,t0)** = Final creep coefficient | **phi_RH** = 1+(1-RH/100)/(0.1*h0^(1/3)) for fcm<=35 MPa | **eps_cd0** = Basic drying shrinkage from Table 6.7 | **kh** = Size factor from Table 6.8 | **eps_ca** = Autogenous shrinkage
standards.notes: IRC 112 mandates full EC2 creep model for bridge design — non-negotiable. Time-dependent effects in bridges: prestress losses (15–25% from creep+shrinkage), differential shrinkage deck-to-beam, creep redistribution in staged construction. Using IS 456 theta values for bridge design is a serious error.

standards.limits: ACI 318 gives minimal guidance — references ACI 209R. Valid for moist-cured concrete loaded after 7 days or steam-cured after 1–3 days.
standards.formula:
phi(t,t0) = (t-t0)^0.6 / (10 + (t-t0)^0.6) * phi_u
phi_u = 2.35 * gamma_c
eps_sh(t) = t/(35+t) * (eps_sh)_u * gamma_sh
standards.notation: **phi_u** = Ultimate creep = 2.35 × product of correction factors gamma_c | **gamma_c** = Corrections for age, humidity, specimen size, slump, fines content, air content, cement content | **eps_sh,u** = Ultimate shrinkage = 780e-6 × gamma_sh | **35** = Time constant for shrinkage development
standards.notes: ACI 209R published 1992 — not updated. Baseline phi_u=2.35 comparable to EC2 for typical conditions. For typical columns (h0=300mm, RH=60%, t0=28d): ACI gives phi~1.8, EC2 gives phi~1.9. Many US engineers now use RILEM B3 or GL2000 models for important structures.

standards.limits: Offshore: RH=70–85% marine atmosphere to RH=100% submerged. Creep coefficients lower due to high humidity.
standards.formula:
phi(inf,t0) = phi_EC2 * k_offshore
k_offshore = 0.70 to 0.85
eps_cs (offshore) ≈ 150–250 × 10^-6
standards.notation: **phi_EC2** = Creep coefficient from EC2 | **k_offshore** = Reduction for high humidity | **eps_cs** = Significantly reduced drying shrinkage due to RH>=70% | **Autogenous shrinkage** = Dominant for HSC offshore (fck 50–70 MPa)
standards.notes: High offshore humidity drastically reduces drying shrinkage — submerged structure may have near-zero drying shrinkage. Autogenous shrinkage becomes dominant for HSC. Long-term prestress loss must be accurately predicted over 30–50 year life for gravity base structures.

concrete_stress_strain.title: Concrete Stress-Strain Relations — Parabolic, Bilinear & Rectangular
concrete_stress_strain.keywords: stress strain stress block parabolic rectangular bilinear Whitney block ultimate strain epsilon cu 0.0035 0.003 concrete model design stress block neutral axis compression zone n factor lambda eta
concrete_stress_strain.description: The stress-strain relation for concrete in compression defines how the compression zone is modelled at ULS. Codes disagree fundamentally — some use the physical parabolic shape, others use a mathematically equivalent rectangle. This choice affects neutral axis depth and moment arm.

standards.clause: Clause 3.1.7 — Three models: (1) Parabolic-rectangular, (2) Bilinear, (3) Rectangular
standards.limits: All three models permitted. For fck > 50 MPa: n, lambda, eta all change — reduced ductility mandatory to account for.
standards.formula:
(1) PARABOLIC-RECTANGULAR:
sigma_c = fcd[1-(1-eps_c/eps_c2)^n]  for 0<=eps_c<=eps_c2
sigma_c = fcd  for eps_c2 < eps_c <= eps_cu2
(2) BILINEAR:
sigma_c = fcd*(eps_c/eps_c3)  for 0<=eps_c<=eps_c3
sigma_c = fcd  for eps_c3 < eps_c <= eps_cu3
(3) RECTANGULAR:
Block depth = lambda*x  ;  sigma_c = eta*fcd
standards.notation: **n** = Shape exponent = 2 for fck<=50 MPa | **eps_c2** = Strain at peak = 0.002 (fck<=50) | **eps_cu2** = Ultimate strain = 0.0035 (fck<=50) | **eps_c3** = End of linear branch (bilinear) = 0.00175 | **eps_cu3** = Ultimate (bilinear/rectangular) = 0.0035 | **lambda** = Block depth factor = 0.8 (fck<=50) | **eta** = Effective strength factor = 1.0 (fck<=50) | All three give essentially identical capacity results
standards.notes: Three models — flexibility for different calculation contexts. Parabolic for research/software; bilinear for spreadsheets; rectangular for hand calc. For fck > 50 MPa: n increases, lambda reduces, eta reduces — HSC is more brittle. This grade-dependent behaviour is absent from IS 456.

standards.clause: Annex B, Fig. B-1 (formerly Clause 38.1, Fig. 21)
standards.limits: Single model only. Parameters fixed regardless of grade — does not account for reduced ductility of HSC above M60.
standards.formula:
sigma_c = fcd[2*(eps_c/0.002) - (eps_c/0.002)^2]  for 0<=eps_c<=0.002
sigma_c = fcd = 0.447*fck  for 0.002 < eps_c <= 0.0035
fcd = 0.67*fck/1.5
standards.notation: **eps_c2** = 0.002 fixed for all grades | **eps_cu** = 0.0035 fixed for all grades | **fcd** = 0.447*fck (44.7% of cube strength) | **n** = 2 (fixed parabola exponent) | Shape identical to EC2 parabolic-rectangular with n=2
standards.notes: Identical shape to EC2 parabolic-rectangular (n=2) — only fcd differs. This IS the model used in the RC capacity tool fibre integration. Fixed eps_cu=0.0035 for all grades is unconservative for M60+ where concrete is more brittle. For WT tower design with HSC, consider EC2 variable parameters.

standards.limits: Same three models as EC2. For fck > 50 MPa, variable eps_cu2, eps_c2, n mandatory.
standards.formula:
Same as EC2 — all three models identical
eps_cu2 = 0.0035  (fck <= 50 MPa)
eps_cu2 = 0.0026 + 0.035*((90-fck)/100)^4  (fck > 50 MPa)
standards.notation: **eps_cu2** = 0.0035 for fck<=50 MPa; reduces above 50 MPa | **eps_c2** = 0.002 (fck<=50) | **n** = 2 (fck<=50); increases above 50 MPa | **lambda** = 0.8 (fck<=50) | **eta** = 1.0 (fck<=50) | **fcd** = 0.67*fck/1.5 (alpha_cc=0.67, NOT 0.85)
standards.notes: Full EC2 framework with grade-dependent parameters for HSC. C60 section: eps_cu2 = 0.0032 (not 0.0035) — reduces compression block depth and moment capacity slightly. Key difference from IS 456: IRC 112 acknowledges HSC brittleness.

standards.limits: eps_cu = 0.003 (14% lower than EC2/IS456's 0.0035). Valid for f'c <= 69 MPa with standard beta1. Above 69 MPa: beta1 = 0.65 minimum.
standards.notation: **eps_cu** = 0.003 (ACI) vs 0.0035 (EC2/IS456) | **a** = Depth of equivalent rectangular stress block | **beta_1** = Ratio of block depth to NA depth: 0.85 (f'c<=28); reduces 0.05 per 7MPa above 28; min 0.65 | **0.85f'c** = Uniform stress of rectangular block | **C** = Total concrete compressive force | No parabola
standards.notes: Whitney rectangular block REPLACES the parabolic shape — it is a mathematical equivalence giving same C force and centroid. Equivalence was empirical for NSC and less accurate for f'c > 55 MPa. ACI eps_cu=0.003 means slightly lower curvature ductility than EC2 but moment capacity difference is <5% for typical sections. beta_1 reduction parallels EC2's eta and lambda.

standards.limits: Rectangular stress block identical to ACI. beta_1 limits same. eps_cu = 0.003.
standards.notation: **Same as ACI 318** — identical rectangular stress block | **eps_cu** = 0.003 | **phi** = 0.9 for flexure (tension-controlled)
standards.notes: AASHTO follows ACI rectangular block. For bridge I-girders and box girders with wide compression flanges, rectangular block is well-suited — compression zone entirely within flange making parabolic vs rectangular academic. 0.003 ultimate strain same as ACI.

standards.limits: Parabolic-rectangular for all grades. Parameters fixed — same limitation as IS 456.
standards.formula:
sigma_c = fcd[1-(1-eps_c/0.002)^2]  for 0<=eps_c<=0.002
sigma_c = fcd = 0.67*fcu/gamma_m  for 0.002 < eps_c <= 0.0035
standards.notation: **fcu** = Characteristic cube strength (MPa) | **gamma_m** = 1.5 | **fcd** = 0.447*fcu | **eps_cu** = 0.0035 | **eps_c2** = 0.002 | Identical formula to IS 456
standards.notes: BS 8110 and IS 456 use identical models — IS 456 was directly derived from BS 8110. Historical lineage: BS 8110 (1985) → IS 456 (2000). Both valid for NSC; both have fixed parameters unconservative for HSC. Both superseded in home markets but widely used on legacy/international projects.

concrete_flexural_tensile_strength.title: Flexural Tensile Strength (Modulus of Rupture) of Concrete
concrete_flexural_tensile_strength.keywords: flexural tensile strength modulus of rupture fctm fctk fct fr tensile strength cracking moment Mcr minimum reinforcement crack control concrete tension split tensile fcr
concrete_flexural_tensile_strength.description: Tensile strength of concrete in flexure (modulus of rupture). Used to determine cracking moment Mcr, minimum reinforcement, shear capacity without reinforcement, tension stiffening in deflection, and crack width calculations.

standards.limits: fctm = mean tensile (minimum reinforcement, crack width). fctk,0.05 = lower 5th percentile (where tension is unfavourable). fctk,0.95 = upper 95th percentile (where tension is favourable e.g. punching shear).
standards.formula:
fctm = 0.30 * fck^(2/3)  (fck <= 50 MPa)
fctm = 2.12 * ln(1 + fcm/10)  (fck > 50 MPa)
fctk,0.05 = 0.7 * fctm
fctk,0.95 = 1.3 * fctm
fctm,fl = max(1.6 - h/1000, 1.0) * fctm
standards.notation: **fctm** = Mean axial tensile strength (MPa) | **fck^(2/3)** = Power law (tensile vs compressive) | **fctk,0.05** = Lower characteristic = 0.7*fctm | **fctk,0.95** = Upper characteristic = 1.3*fctm | **fctm,fl** = Mean flexural tensile (modulus of rupture) — higher than axial due to stress gradient | **h** = Overall section depth (mm) — size effect | **Example C35**: fctm = 0.30*35^(2/3) = 3.21 MPa
standards.notes: EC2 distinguishes three tensile strength values. Size effect (1.6-h/1000) is important — deeper beams have lower flexural tensile strength. For h=200mm: fctm,fl = 1.4*fctm (40% higher for shallow members). For h=600mm: fctm,fl = fctm. Size effect absent from IS 456 and ACI.

standards.limits: Single value fcr used for cracking moment and deflection. No percentile distinction. No size effect.
standards.notation: **fcr** = Flexural tensile strength / modulus of rupture (MPa) | **fck** = Characteristic cube strength (MPa) | **0.7** = Empirical coefficient | **Example M35**: fcr = 0.7*sqrt(35) = 4.14 MPa | Note: This is flexural value — do NOT compare directly to EC2 fctm (axial); compare to EC2 fctm,fl
standards.notes: IS 456 fcr is a flexural value — higher than EC2 fctm because EC2 fctm is axial. Compare IS fcr to EC2 fctm,fl only. No size effect means IS 456 overestimates cracking moment for deep sections. Used for: cracking moment, deflection (Annex C Cl.C-2), and minimum reinforcement checks.

standards.limits: Same as EC2 — fctm, fctk,0.05, fctk,0.95 all used in different checks. Minimum reinforcement uses fctk,0.05 (more conservative than EC2 buildings).
standards.formula:
fctm = 0.30 * fck^(2/3)  (fck <= 50 MPa)
fctm = 2.12 * ln(1 + fcm/10)  (fck > 50 MPa)
As,min = 0.26 * (fctm/fyk) * bt * d >= 0.0013*bt*d
standards.notation: **fctm** = Mean tensile — same formula as EC2 | **fctk,0.05** = 0.7*fctm | **As,min** = Minimum reinforcement | **bt** = Mean width of tension zone | **d** = Effective depth | Note: IRC 112 minimum grade fck>=30 MPa automatically gives higher fctm
standards.notes: IRC 112 adopts EC2 tensile framework completely. For uncracked SLS check: use fctk,0.05 (conservative lower bound) — what IRC 112 mandates in certain cases. Deck slabs crack from restrained shrinkage — using fctm for minimum reinforcement is appropriate since cracking occurs on average.

standards.limits: fr used for deflection (Mcr), minimum flexural reinforcement, cracked section analysis. Split cylinder fct ≈ 0.56*sqrt(f'c) for direct tension (ACI Commentary).
standards.formula:
f_r = 0.62 * lambda * sqrt(f'_c)  (MPa)
f_ct ≈ 0.56 * lambda * sqrt(f'_c)  (split cylinder)
standards.notation: **fr** = Modulus of rupture — flexural tensile strength (MPa) | **f'c** = Cylinder strength (MPa) | **lambda** = 1.0 normal weight; 0.85 sand-lightweight; 0.75 all-lightweight | **0.62** = Empirical coefficient | **Example f'c=28**: fr = 0.62*sqrt(28) = 3.28 MPa | **Mcr** = fr * Ig / yt
standards.notes: ACI lambda factor for lightweight concrete is significant practical advantage — IS 456 has no equivalent reduction. IS M30 gives fcr=3.83 MPa; ACI equivalent f'c=24 MPa gives fr=3.04 MPa. Difference partly reflects cube vs cylinder basis. Mcr used extensively in effective moment of inertia Ie for deflection.

standards.limits: fr for cracked section analysis and minimum reinforcement. Minimum reinforcement: section must resist 1.2*Mcr or 1.33*Mu whichever is less.
standards.notation: **fr** = Modulus of rupture (MPa) | **lambda** = 1.0 normal weight | **0.63** = Slightly higher than ACI's 0.62 (better QC on bridge concrete) | **Mcr** = fr * Sc where Sc = section modulus at extreme tension fibre | **Minimum reinforcement**: 1.2*Mcr or 1.33*Mu
standards.notes: AASHTO 0.63 marginally higher than ACI 0.62 — reflecting better QC expected for bridge concrete. Minimum reinforcement rule (1.2*Mcr or 1.33*Mu) more explicit than IS 456 — prevents sudden brittle failure at first crack, critical for bridges with no flexural redundancy.

standards.limits: Uses lower characteristic fctk for design — not mean fctm. Reflects consequence of cracking in offshore environment (seawater ingress initiates corrosion).
standards.formula:
fctk = 0.7 * fctm = 0.7 * 0.30 * fck^(2/3)
fctd = fctk / gamma_c = fctk / 1.5
standards.notation: **fctk** = Lower characteristic tensile = 0.7*fctm | **fctm** = Mean tensile from EC2 formula | **fctd** = Design tensile = fctk/gamma_c | **Note**: DNV uses fctk for design (not fctm) — more conservative than EC2 buildings
standards.notes: DNV uses lower characteristic fctk for all tension design checks — deliberate conservatism. Offshore cracking allows seawater ingress initiating chloride-driven corrosion, virtually impossible to repair. For C40 offshore: fctm=3.51 MPa, fctk=2.46 MPa, fctd=1.64 MPa — drives significantly more minimum reinforcement than equivalent onshore EC2 design.
